title: Urinary Tract Obstruction
subject: Pathology
summary: Post‑renal obstruction blocks urine flow, causing hydronephrosis, impaired renal function and risk of infection. Prompt recognition and relief are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: A blockage anywhere from the renal pelvis to the urethral meatus that prevents normal urine outflow, leading to back‑pressure, hydronephrosis and possible acute kidney injury.
b: Diagnosis requires suspicion from history, physical exam and imaging (ultrasound preferred).
Absence of urine output <400 mL/24 h suggests obstruction in acute settings.

t.b: Does the kidney show hydronephrosis? – Positive result confirms obstructive dilatation; negative suggests non‑obstructive causes.
Is renal function falling after obstruction? – Rising creatinine supports post‑renal azotemia; if unavailable, monitor urine output.

sections.p: Severity is graded by degree of hydronephrosis and renal function loss.
b: Mild: Grade 1–2 hydronephrosis, creatinine rise <0.3 mg/dL after obstruction.
Moderate: Grade 3 hydronephrosis, creatinine rise 0.3–0.6 mg/dL, oliguria.
Severe: Grade 4 hydronephrosis, creatinine rise >0.6 mg/dL, anuria or output <400 mL/24 h.

sections.p: Identify the level of blockage and common aetiologies in East African hospitals.
b: Ureteric stones (calcium oxalate, uric acid, endemic schistosomal calcifications).
Urethral stricture from prior infection, trauma or herbal remedies.
External compression by pelvic malignancy (cervical, prostate, bladder cancer).
Pregnancy‑related uterine compression.
Tuberculosis of the genitourinary tract.
Severe prostatic hypertrophy, especially in HIV‑positive men.

sections.p: Patients develop flank or suprapubic pain, reduced urine output and systemic signs if infection supervenes.
b: Colicky flank pain radiating to groin.
Visible bladder distension in lower‑tract obstruction.
Nausea, vomiting, fever if secondary infection.
History of stone passage, prior surgery, or HIV/TB.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there hydronephrosis? – Positive confirms obstruction; if unavailable, rely on clinical bladder palpation and creatinine trend.
Is infection present? – Positive leukocyte esterase or bacteria indicates secondary UTI, guiding antibiotics.
Are there signs of acute kidney injury? – Rising urea/creatinine and hyperkalaemia demand urgent decompression.
Are radio‑opaque stones visible? – Detects large calculi when ultrasound not feasible.

sections.p: Unchecked obstruction rapidly damages renal parenchyma and can precipitate sepsis.
b: Anuria or output <400 mL/24 h.
Rapid creatinine rise >0.5 mg/dL in 24 h.
Fever >38 °C with flank pain – suspect infected hydronephrosis.
Persistent pain despite analgesia – possible papillary necrosis.

sections.p: Relieve the blockage first, then treat infection and support renal function.
b: Ureteric stones ≤5 mm: trial of passage with hydration; if fails, refer for ureteroscopy or lithotripsy.
Large stones or failed passage: percutaneous nephrostomy (if surgical expertise present) or emergency cystoscopy with stent placement.
Urethral stricture: gentle catheterisation, then referral for urethroplasty; avoid forceful dilation to prevent false passage.
Infection: start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) after cultures; adjust for local resistance patterns.
Supportive: monitor urine output, correct electrolytes, avoid nephrotoxic drugs.

sections.p: Ensure patency, treat underlying disease and educate on hydration.
b: Repeat ultrasound 2‑4 weeks after decompression to confirm resolution.
Metabolic work‑up for recurrent stones (uric acid, calcium) when resources allow.
Counsel on adequate fluid intake (≥2 L/day) and avoidance of herbal urethral inserts.
Screen for TB or HIV in patients with atypical strictures.
Acute pyelonephritis – pain and fever but no hydronephrosis.
Renal colic from non‑obstructive ureteric spasm – pain resolves quickly, imaging negative.
Bladder tumour – suprapubic mass with urinary retention, but ultrasound shows mass rather than dilated ureters.
Normal creatinine early in obstruction – urine output is a more reliable early marker.
Ultrasound may miss small distal ureteric stones; consider KUB or CT if available.
Low‑grade fever may be absent in immunocompromised patients; maintain suspicion for infected hydronephrosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Anuria or urine output <400 mL/24 h
Rapid rise in serum creatinine >0.5 mg/dL within 24 h

faq.q: Can a patient have normal urine output with obstruction?
faq.a: Early obstruction may preserve output; monitor trends and imaging rather than rely on volume alone.

faq.q: Why is a nephrostomy preferred over a stent in some cases?
faq.a: Nephrostomy bypasses the entire ureter, useful when the ureter is severely damaged or inaccessible.

faq.q: Is prophylactic antibiotics needed after stone removal?
faq.a: Only if there was documented infection or significant urinary stasis; otherwise routine prophylaxis is not recommended.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with flank pain and output 300 mL/24 h. What is your next step? — Perform bedside ultrasound to look for hydronephrosis; if positive, arrange urgent decompression.
How does post‑renal azotemia differ biochemically from intrinsic AKI? — BUN/creatinine ratio often >20:1 early, and urine sodium is low; obstruction shows rapid reversal after relief.
What imaging modality is most feasible in a district hospital and why? — Renal ultrasound because it is portable, radiation‑free and detects hydronephrosis.

A patient with a known urethral stricture develops suprapubic tenderness. Which complication should you anticipate? — Infected hydronephrosis; start empiric antibiotics and plan for catheter drainage.
Why is forceful catheterisation contraindicated in suspected urethral stricture? — It can create a false passage, worsening obstruction and causing bleeding.
Explain why serum creatinine may be misleading in early obstruction. — Creatinine rises only after significant nephron loss; urine output and imaging are earlier indicators.

What are the key elements of long‑term prevention for recurrent stones in this setting? — Adequate hydration, dietary calcium balance, treat hyperuricemia if present, and screen for metabolic disorders when possible.

Distinguish obstructive uropathy from acute pyelonephritis on exam and bedside tests. — Obstruction shows flank tenderness with a palpable kidney or hydronephrosis on ultrasound; pyelonephritis has fever, CVA tenderness but normal ultrasound.
